name: Bistre Green
lede: Bistre Green is a muted golden yellow, named for bistre, the brown soot pigment artists once drew with, and first recorded by Maerz and Paul in 1905.

sections.title: A drawing pigment's name
sections.body: The nearest named colors on file are [[olive-ocher]], [[light-cadmium]], [[pyrite-yellow]] and [[tennis]], at 2.7, 2.9, 2.9 and 3.5 ΔE [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system would class a close match as dark yellow, about 2.3 units of ΔE away [1]. The swatch is a yellow, not the brown of bistre itself, so the name points to the pigment family rather than its color [1]. In LCH terms it is a mid-light, strongly chromatic gold: lightness 70, chroma 47, hue 91 degrees [1]. A fifth, slightly farther neighbor is [[popcorn]], 4.1 ΔE away, lighter [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings finds a close match to Bistre Green in 774, about 3.3 percent, as photographed [2]. It covers most of the frame in Japanese woodblock prints: Hiroshige's *Matsuchiyama on the Sumida River* (1833) at 77 percent and Hokusai's *Moon, Pine and Maple* at 73 percent [2]. Among Western painters it is used most, relative to their own baselines, by Henry Raeburn and Paul Sérusier, and its peak decade is the 1930s, though only 7 of 69 paintings from then carry it [2].

origin.source: Maerz and Paul, A Dictionary of Color; ColorHub library
